items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Well Charlie Christian, I mean when I first heard him I was just absolutely stunned... So when I heard him and it got to me so then I started playing from playing a million notes to playing almost no notes.

ctx.x: Explain his influence and then talk about how the jazz guitar has evolved from that time.

Well Charlie Christian, I mean when I first heard him I was just absolutely stunned you know. And I was a kid at that time and I could play a lot of notes, I mean a lot of notes, but they were worthless you know. So when I heard him and it got to me so then I started playing from playing a million notes to playing almost no notes. I mean each note had to be sent to me directly from heaven before I would consider playing it. And somewhere in there I’ve struck a happy medium. And Charlie changed the whole nature of…
That’s another theme in jazz is the early and tragic death of some of its greatest players.

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Absolutely. And Django Rinehardt to some degree, but Charlie was the biggest influence.

ctx.x: Would you say that Charlie Christian was an influence for you?
Absolutely. And Django Rinehardt to some degree, but Charlie was the biggest influence.
How many opportunities did you have to see him?
